title: Transactions
summary: How transactions group reads and writes into an all-or-nothing unit to simplify error handling and concurrency, the weak isolation levels that trade correctness for performance, the race conditions each prevents, and the three routes to true serializability.
keyTakeaways: ACID: Atomicity = abortability (all-or-nothing on failure), Consistency = an app-level invariant (the odd one out, the app's responsibility), Isolation = concurrent transactions don't interfere, Durability = committed data survives.
Read committed prevents dirty reads and dirty writes; snapshot isolation (MVCC) additionally prevents read skew by giving each transaction a consistent point-in-time view.
Lost updates need atomic ops, explicit locking (SELECT FOR UPDATE), automatic detect-and-abort, or compare-and-set; replication with LWW silently loses updates.
Write skew is a generalized race where two transactions read the same objects then update different ones (e.g., on-call doctors); phantoms are writes that change another transaction's search result.
Serializability has three implementations: actual serial execution (single-threaded + stored procedures), two-phase locking (2PL), and serializable snapshot isolation (SSI, optimistic).
Do not confuse 2PL (a locking concurrency-control method for isolation) with 2PC (two-phase commit, an atomic-commit protocol).

questions.q: In ACID, which property is best described as 'abortability' — the ability to discard all of a transaction's writes if anything goes wrong partway through?
options: Consistency
Isolation
Atomicity
Durability
questions.explain: DDIA frames atomicity as abortability: on failure the transaction is aborted and all its partial writes are thrown away, so it's all-or-nothing. Durability is about committed data surviving crashes; isolation is about concurrency.

questions.q: Why does DDIA call the 'C' (Consistency) in ACID the odd one out?
options: It refers to application-level invariants the application must maintain, not a guarantee the database provides — unlike A, I, and D
It is the only property that is impossible to implement
It is a synonym for isolation and thus redundant
It only applies to replicated databases
questions.explain: Consistency here means the data satisfies application-defined invariants; the database can only help, but it's the application's job to define and preserve them. Atomicity, isolation, and durability are genuinely database-provided.

options: A fully consistent snapshot of the entire database for the transaction's lifetime
That transactions execute as if one at a time
That lost updates cannot occur
No dirty reads and no dirty writes — you only read/overwrite committed data
questions.explain: Read committed prevents dirty reads (seeing uncommitted data) and dirty writes (overwriting uncommitted data). A consistent point-in-time snapshot is snapshot isolation, a stronger level; read committed does not prevent lost updates or read skew.

questions.q: How is read committed typically implemented for reads and writes?
options: A single global lock serializes all transactions
Row-level locks prevent dirty writes, while for reads the database remembers and returns the old committed value until the new one commits (rather than holding read locks)
Multi-version snapshots keyed to a transaction start timestamp
Optimistic detection that aborts on conflict
questions.explain: Write locks per object prevent dirty writes; for reads, holding locks would hurt throughput, so the DB serves the last committed value until the writer commits. Full multi-version snapshots per transaction are how snapshot isolation (a stronger level) works.

questions.q: What race condition does snapshot isolation specifically prevent that read committed does not?
options: Dirty writes
Write skew
Read skew (nonrepeatable read) — a transaction seeing different parts of the database at different points in time
Phantom reads in all cases
questions.explain: Snapshot isolation gives the whole transaction one consistent point-in-time view, preventing read skew where, mid-transaction, you'd see some data pre-update and some post-update. It still does not prevent write skew or all phantoms.

questions.q: What is the core mechanism behind snapshot isolation, and what property does it give readers vs. writers?
options: Two-phase locking; readers and writers both block each other
A single serial execution thread; no concurrency at all
Compare-and-set on every read
Multi-version concurrency control (MVCC); readers never block writers and writers never block readers
questions.explain: Snapshot isolation uses MVCC, keeping multiple committed versions so each transaction reads from a consistent snapshot without blocking writers (and vice versa). This makes it ideal for long-running reads like backups and analytics.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a valid technique for preventing lost updates?
options: Enabling last-write-wins conflict resolution on a replicated database
Atomic write operations (e.g., a single UPDATE ... SET x = x + 1)
Explicit locking with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
Compare-and-set (only write if the value hasn't changed since you read it)
questions.explain: Atomic ops, explicit locks, and compare-and-set all prevent lost updates; automatic detect-and-abort does too. LWW on replicated systems is explicitly called out as a way lost updates still happen, because it discards concurrent writes.

questions.q: Which scenario is the textbook example of write skew?
options: Two users both incrementing the same counter and one increment being lost
Two on-call doctors each checking that at least one other doctor is on call, then both simultaneously booking off — leaving no one on call
A transaction reading uncommitted data from another transaction
A backup reading rows at different times mid-transaction
questions.explain: Write skew: two transactions read the same set (doctors on call), each sees the invariant satisfied, then each updates a different row, together violating the invariant. The counter case is a classic lost update, not write skew.

questions.q: In DDIA's terminology, what is a 'phantom'?
options: A committed write that vanishes after a crash
A replica that reports itself as leader after failover
A write in one transaction that changes the result of a search query in another transaction
A read that returns uncommitted data
questions.explain: A phantom occurs when one transaction's write alters the set of rows another transaction's WHERE-clause search would match, causing write skew. Snapshot isolation can't lock rows that don't yet exist; 'materializing conflicts' is one workaround.

questions.q: What is the key requirement that makes 'actual serial execution' (single-threaded transactions, as in VoltDB/Redis) viable?
options: Extremely fast disks so every transaction can be fsynced individually
A cluster of at least five nodes for quorum
Predicate locks on every index range
The active dataset must fit in memory and transactions must be short (often stored procedures), with writes partitionable for throughput
questions.explain: Running transactions one at a time on a single thread only works if data is in RAM (no disk-wait stalls) and transactions are small stored procedures; throughput scales by partitioning. Predicate/index-range locks belong to 2PL, a different approach.

questions.q: Two-phase locking (2PL) enforces serializability using which locking scheme?
options: Shared (read) and exclusive (write) locks, where readers block writers and writers block everyone — plus predicate or index-range locks to prevent phantoms
A single global mutex held for the whole transaction
Optimistic locks acquired only at commit time
Compare-and-set on each written row
questions.explain: 2PL uses shared/exclusive locks so reads and writes mutually block, and adds predicate/index-range locks to stop phantoms. Its downsides are poor performance (lots of blocking) and deadlocks; optimistic-at-commit describes SSI, not 2PL.

questions.q: How does serializable snapshot isolation (SSI) differ from two-phase locking?
options: SSI is pessimistic and locks earlier than 2PL
SSI is optimistic: transactions run without blocking on a snapshot, and at commit the database checks whether reads were invalidated by concurrent writes, aborting if so
SSI abandons snapshot isolation entirely
SSI can only run on a single thread
questions.explain: SSI lets transactions proceed optimistically on a consistent snapshot and detects serialization conflicts (stale premises) at commit, aborting the loser. This avoids 2PL's heavy locking and generally scales better, at the cost of wasted work on aborts.

questions.q: Why does DDIA warn readers not to confuse 2PL with 2PC?
options: They are the same protocol under two names
2PC provides isolation and 2PL provides atomicity
Both are consensus algorithms like Paxos
2PL (two-phase locking) is a concurrency-control method for isolation, whereas 2PC (two-phase commit) is an atomic-commit protocol across nodes — different problems entirely
questions.explain: The names are similar but unrelated: 2PL is about serializable isolation via locks (this chapter), while 2PC is about committing a distributed transaction atomically across participants (Chapter 9). Conflating them is a common exam trap.

questions.q: What is the practical relationship between single-object and multi-object operations regarding transactions?
options: Single-object atomicity/isolation is common even in non-transactional stores, but coordinating an invariant across multiple objects is what genuinely requires multi-object transactions
Multi-object transactions are unnecessary because single-object atomicity covers everything
Single-object operations always require distributed consensus
Multi-object transactions only matter for read-only workloads
questions.explain: Many datastores provide atomic single-object writes cheaply, but keeping an invariant consistent across several rows/documents (e.g., moving money between accounts, updating denormalized copies) is exactly where multi-object transactions earn their keep.
